questions.q: What are the two pieces of a passé composé?
choices: An auxiliary in the present plus a past participle
questions.why: Avoir or être in the present tense, then the past participle. Everything hard about the tense is choosing the auxiliary and deciding on agreement.
The regular system is -er → -é, -ir → -i, -re → -u. So parlé, fini, vendu.
Écrire gives écrit, in the -it / -ert pile with dit, fait, ouvert and offert. Écris is the present tense of je or tu.

questions.q: Type what you hear, in correct written French.
questions.why: Pas sits between the auxiliary and the participle. Note n' before the vowel of ai.
Every reflexive takes être without exception, plus the DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP list of intransitive movement and change-of-state verbs.
Monter, descendre, sortir, rentrer, retourner and passer switch to avoir when a direct object follows, and the meaning shifts too: he took the suitcases up, not he went up.

questions.q: Put it in the past: « Elle va au marché. » → Elle ___ au marché.
questions.why: Aller takes être, so the participle agrees with the feminine singular subject: allée.
With avoir the default is no agreement at all. The object les pommes comes after the verb, so nothing changes.

questions.q: Agreement: « Les pommes ? Je les ai (manger) ___ . »
questions.why: A direct object placed before the verb triggers agreement with avoir. Here the pronoun les stands for les pommes: feminine plural, so mangées.

questions.q: Why is « Je leur ai parlé » not « parlés » ?
choices: Leur is an indirect object, and an indirect object never triggers agreement
questions.why: Only a preceding direct object triggers agreement. Parler à takes an indirect object, so the participle stays flat.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I didn't see it. (it = le film)
questions.why: The object pronoun goes before the auxiliary, inside the ne … pas sandwich. Le film is masculine singular, so no agreement is visible on vu.

questions.q: Build the sentence: We didn't wash. (nous, se laver)
questions.why: Reflexive, so être; ne … pas wraps the auxiliary with the reflexive pronoun tucked in before it; se is the direct object, so the participle agrees: lavés.
Les mains is the direct object and comes after the verb, so se is only indirect and nothing agrees. Compare elle s'est lavée, with no object.

questions.q: State the agreement rule for avoir, for être, and for reflexives, in one sentence each.
a: Avoir: no agreement, unless a direct object comes before the verb (je les ai mangées). Être: the participle agrees with the subject (elles sont allées). Reflexives: they use être but follow the avoir rule, agreeing only when the reflexive pronoun is itself the direct object (elle s'est lavée, but elle s'est lavé les mains).
questions.why: The three rules collapse into one question worth asking every time: is there a direct object, and does it come before the verb?

questions.q: Say this out loud: she went to the market.
questions.why: Aller takes être and the participle agrees with the subject, though the extra -e of allée changes nothing you can hear.
